trigger: Microsoft 365 migration under consideration for next financial year

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Tom Reid, it's Jordan from Harbourline IT. I know Meridian AI has grown quickly in Richmond. What made you take a call about managed IT now?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: We're at one hundred and eighteen people and the tooling is catching up with us. Engineering is fine, but the rest of the company is spread across Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 trials, a few SaaS admin accounts and a lot of tribal knowledge.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Where is that mess causing the most friction today?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: Onboarding and access reviews. New starters get a laptop quickly, but permissions depend on which team lead remembered which checklist. Finance also wants more predictable support, because engineers are tired of being unofficial helpdesk.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Who owns the decision if you move from the current hybrid setup to a cleaner Microsoft 365 environment?

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: I can recommend the technical approach, but finance owns budget and the COO owns timing. Neither is on this call. I'm gathering options before next year planning.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Harbourline can run the migration, then support everyone under a managed services agreement. For a company at your size, the monthly fee would likely land around $145 per seat, with a project for tenant design, identity and device management.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: Budget sits with finance next financial year, not with me this month. I do not want a proposal that assumes authority I do not have.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Totally, although it's helpful to get a number in front of people early. If finance sees the risk and productivity case, they can make room before the planning cycle closes.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: Maybe. My bigger concern is whether an external provider can work with engineers without slowing us down. We've unusual device needs, Linux boxes, lab environments and a strong preference for not being locked down blindly.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: We're flexible. We can segment engineering and corporate users, apply different policies and still keep reporting clean. The important thing is having a central support channel and clear admin ownership.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: That sounds plausible, but I'd need our platform lead in the detail. Also, this isn't urgent in September. It's a next financial year budget conversation unless something breaks.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Understood. We've done Microsoft 365 migrations where engineering teams keep the workflows they need while the rest of the business gets structure. I can show examples in a deck.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: Examples would be fine, but decks have a way of floating around Slack and dying. If there's a specific workshop later, I can bring finance and platform.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: Let me send a capability deck and a rough migration outline. You can share it with finance and the COO, and then we can see whether a workshop makes sense.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: Okay, send it through. I'm not promising a workshop yet. I need to see if the business wants to do anything before November.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: That's fair. I will also include an indicative timeline and the questions we'd need answered before pricing the onboarding project.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: Good. Keep it brief, please. If it's twenty pages, nobody here will read it.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: One option is a discovery workshop rather than a full proposal. We could map users, systems, admin ownership and migration risks, then give finance a budget range for next year.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: That sounds closer to what we need, but I still need the COO to agree it's worth a workshop. We've a lot of competing planning work.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: I will frame the outline as a decision brief rather than a sales proposal, with the risks of doing nothing, a staged migration path and the questions finance should answer.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: That would travel better internally. People here react badly to vendor language, but a decision brief with open questions could get read.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: If the brief gets traction, the best next call would include finance, the COO and your platform lead so we can separate commercial timing from technical concerns.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: Agreed. Without those people, we'd just have another interesting conversation that doesn't move anything.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: I will keep the brief anchored to your growth problem rather than pretending this is an emergency. The question is whether the current informal support model can survive another hiring cycle.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: That's the right question. We can survive this month, but another burst of hiring would expose the access and onboarding problems again.

turns.speaker: rep
turns.name: Jordan Lee
turns.text: I will keep it to the essentials and follow up after you've had a chance to circulate it.

turns.speaker: prospect
turns.name: Tom Reid
turns.text: Thanks Jordan. There's interest, just no firm path yet.
